speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had just concluded making some references to the suggested guidelines arising from the conference on pollution and our environment which was held recently in Montreal. I referred in particular to those guidelines which I felt had a direct relevance to the item now under consideration, namely, the administration of the National Research Council.
I would now like to attempt to relate what I was saying earlier directly to the operation of the N.R.C., and to do so I would like to make one or two references to the publications of that body. I am referring to a booklet entitled "N.R.C. Yesterday Today Tomorrow" which was published on the occasion of the fiftieth

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
anniversary of the founding of the council in 1916.
I am referring to the booklet for two reasons. First, I believe that we as members of this house should accept a greater responsibility than we have in the past for assisting the Canadian people to know and to understand the asset they have in the National Research Council which has been built up over the last 50 years and, second, I feel that in the urgency of approaching a solution to the growing pollution problem in Canada we should first take a look at the resources we have at hand which can be put to work in this field, and I hope to suggest that N.R.C. is indeed a very important agency which we could use in this connection. I will therefore quote from the publication to which I referred. On page 1 it reads:
The National Research Council of Canada Is a link between the scientific interests of the government, industry and the universities of Canada and a patron of basic and applied science. The governing body of the council is drawn from leading members of the universities, industries and labour. Research
N.R.C.'s ten laboratory divisions in Ottawa and two regional institutions, one in Halifax, and one in Saskatoon, comprise Canada's largest and most diversified laboratory complex.
Both pure and long-term applied research are carried out in these laboratories, as well as contract research on specific projects, standardization work, and testing for which no private or commercial facilities are available.
A little farther on, under the heading "Technical Information", it reads as follows:
N.R.C.'s technical information service provides, without cost, information and advice on technological matters to Canadian firms. Its industrial engineers give direct assistance and advice especially to small firms on improvement of their plant layout, efficiency of operating and good plant management. This service answers about 17,000 inquiries per year from Canadian industries.
It seems to me that this is a very short but effective summary of the work done by N.R.C. It also seems to me that N.R.C. is the kind of institution which was certainly uppermost in the minds of the numerous technically competent people and people from various federal and provincial government departments who attended the conference in Montreal. It is an institution which is in the position to serve the government, industry and universities in relation to research in the pollution field. I would therefore suggest that although there is no provision in these estimates for the kind of work suggested in the guidelines which arose from the conference on pollution, nevertheless now is the time to start preparing for consideration of next year's estimates in which

appropriate provision may have to be made for work in the field of pollution similar to what the N.R.C. is already doing in many other fields. We should expect to see a major expansion in the very limited work in this field that already comes within the responsibility of the National Research Council.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It is not my intention at this time to go into any detail as to the discussions to which I listened with regard to the amount of money that needs to be put into the battle against pollution. I might mention in passing that one of the spokesmen at the conference, in order to give us some idea of the scale on which the war against pollution should be fought, suggested that if we were to put into it something equivalent to the amount now appropriated for the national defences forces of Canada we would be thinking in terms of the kind of scale on which this problem should be attacked. What I particularly want to emphasize is that we should begin to think about taking active steps to commence this program.
One of the reasons I am taking the opportunity of emphasizing this matter on the discussion of the estimates of the National Research Council is that during my visit to the Montreal road establishment not too long ago one of the places we were taken to see was the division of building research. We had some discussion about the work of that division, about its relationship to the national building code of Canada and the kind of co-operation that existed between it and a body like Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in regard to the improvement of building standards throughout Canada.
During the week I was in Montreal the picture that built up in my mind in respect of the operations of the building research division and the national building code came back to me several times. Increasingly as I listened to the discussion it seemed to me that the most appropriate way to approach the idea of a national pollution standards code or whatever one might eventually decide to call it, for the practical implementation across the country of pollution control in a manner which would bring about co-operation between all levels of government in Canada was already established in an ideal pattern within the existing framework of the National Research Council.
I should like to make a brief reference to the work of the division of building research in relation to the national building code as outlined in the 1965-66 annual report of the
November 17, 1966

council. At page 26 of that report the following paragraph appears:
The division of building research, in its continuing service to Canada's largest industry, serves the whole field of design and construction. This includes not only problems associated with superstructure design, but also questions related to the design of foundations and to the ground on which structures and buildings have to be founded.
Soil mechanics and allied studies, grouped under the title Geotechnical Research, continue, therefore, to occupy an important place in the program of work of the division.
On the same page under the heading "Code" I find the following:
The national building code of Canada provides probably the most important bridge between research and practice. Although published through the associate committee on the national building code, the code reflects many of the most recent findings from the division's work.
Early in 1965, the fourth (new) edition of the code was published. Before the end of the year the first printing of 10,000 copies was almost exhausted, indicating the wide acceptance of the code across Canada. By local legal adoption, it is now in official use from coast to coast by 80 per cent of the cities of Canada, and for the direct benefit of about 70 per cent of the total urban population.
New adoptions of the code are continuing so that the time is not far distant when Canada will have essential technical uniformity in all its local building regulations, through the voluntary adoption of a publication of the National Research Council firmly based upon the results of building research.
It seems to me that if what is described there in respect of the division of building research and the national building code, the adoption of which has spread across Canada, could be translated into terms of developing standards and implementing controls in the field of pollution, it could provide almost an ideal parallel. As I said earlier in my remarks, the general consensus of the conference was that the field of enforcement and administration of pollution control properly rests, constitutionally and otherwise, primarily in the hands of the provincial authorities, and through them is applied to the municipal or regional divisions of the country.
However, there was general agreement, which certainly confirmed the view I have held for quite some time, that the only way in which this whole problem can be really attacked in a proper manner is if we in this parliament, through the federal government, exercise real leadership and guidance. Only when we can develop a national code and national standards based upon active and continuing research, so that the standards can be continually upgraded as new science and technology are developed, can we make continuing progress in this field which will lead to
Supply-Industry
more uniformity across the entire country, thereby avoiding all the complications in the various fields of industry because of the existence of different standards in different regions or provinces of the country.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that if nothing more has emerged out of that conference than this, certainly the most logical guideline that can be actively implemented with the least possible delay, we should utilize the existing framework of the national research council to establish a national pollution control institute and through that institute develop a national pollution standards code. Backed by the kind of work done in the field of building research we could continually upgrade our approach in dealing with this whole problem.
The most knowledgeable spokesmen at the conference suggested that most of the research on the technical problems of the control of domestic sewage or waste had been donej but continually reference was made to what some described as the more exotic chemical compounds that increasingly emanate from developing industry. I do not know whether some of the chemicals that emanate from some industrial plants in my constituency could be described as exotic, but they are certainly chemicals that a great many of my constituents would prefer to see somewhere else than in the air or water of the region in which they live. The truth of what I say is obvious to all of us, and applies to more and more parts of our country as time goes on.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I join with the hon. member for Kootenay West in urging on the minister and the house the view that no time ought to be lost. The guidelines from the conference and the spirit and interest generated must not be lost. We in this house should accept our share of responsibility for seeing that they are not lost.
We cannot afford delay. I know that what I am about to mention is not directly parallel with the facts, but because of experience in this house I must take advantage of the first opportunity to raise some of these matters in the aftermath of the conference. I am not indulging in political gibes, but I recall that not too long ago a debate, not concluded yet, was begun in this house and reference was made to guidelines in the field of medical care which were laid down in 1919. With that background in mind I hope that hon. members now occupying the treasury benches will take a somewhat different approach to implement

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
the guide lines of the conference on pollution in our environment held earlier this year.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on item 10. I thought we could give the minister a sense of accomplishment if we left vote 1 and went to vote 10. I want to say a few words about the Medical Research Council, the grants proposed for the coming year and those given in the past year. I was pleased to hear the increase that the minister has recommended but I am sorry to say, as has been said by others this afternoon and this evening, that it is not good enough. It is too little. The minister obviously has not paid attention to the many organizations and reports advocating increased grants for medical research, particularly in view of the medical care legislation which we hope to have before the house at some time, though the prospects are somewhat dim at the moment. Nevertheless, I submit that the house and the government must take a longer and closer look at the reasons for the shortages of funds for medical research in Canada.
My colleague from Simcoe East points out that in the United States they spend $5.05 per capita on medical research whereas we spend about 75 cents per capita. This is not good enough. As an example I should like to show how badly the University of Saskatchewan medical school, my home college, needs money and help in the field of medical research. Quite recently there was a long series of articles in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, beginning on October 29 and running through to November 2 on the problem of the financing of research as a major health need. I wish to quote from the excellent articles written by a staff reporter, Florence Pratt.
More and better teachers and better facilities for research, or second class medical care-which?
I hope that is a rhetorical question.
This is the critical situation which medical personnel and some laymen say Canada must face at once.

She quotes Dr. Louis Horlick of the department of clinical medicine in the university medical school.
-to provide high class service, "the kind I am convinced the people of Canada want, we must produce a new kind of doctor, one who will not be obsolete the day he graduates. He must know how to receive information and use it properly. This calls for a new kind of training-one that will teach the student how to examine, evaluate and apply evidence and treatment."
Sound teaching and research go hand in hand. They require a medical college which both teaches and carries on a continuing research program, interfaculty exchange of ideas and continual expansion of those ideas-*
The article points out that it is not enough to find one or two qualified men. Then it continues:
A researcher coming here needs to be assured conditions, both of staff and of facilities, will stimulate and encourage the creative mind.
A favourable climate for research is a nebulous thing, formed of a well-balanced combination of people, equipment and buildings. This combination can be provided. But it takes money, a great deal of money and long-range planning. In Canada, the immediate and most urgent problem is where and how to get that money.
Though I am pleased at the proposed 33J per cent increase, it is about 50 per cent of what is required at this time and perhaps 20 per cent of what will be needed in ten years if, as the hon. member for Simcoe East points out, we are to bring in the kind of medical teachers who have solid research backgrounds and can produce more and better doctors to service Canada's people, and if we are to stop the exodus of doctors to the United States and other countries. We must have these funds and we must have them now.
We are all familiar with the Gundy report which was presented to the Prime Minister earlier this year. Surely the minister knows what the Gundy report recommends should be spent on research. If he has not done so I suggest that he should read the report, as it makes excellent reading and is most informative. The summary of the report on page 1 says:
Medical research is essential to the provision of high standards of medical education, health services and health care. This fact must be recognized in any programs aimed at broadening health services and raising health care standards in Canada. If these are to become objectives of public policy-
We all know, if I may interject my thought, that this matter ought indeed to become one of the objectives of this house. It continues:
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
-provision must be made for expansion of medical education in Canada and this, in turn, necessitates a greatly expanded scale of medical research effort.
November 17, 1966

It is, of course, the Gundy report which suggests a minimum of $40 million rather than the $15 million or $20 million, if there is an increase, that is now being provided. I see the figure given in vote No. 10 is $12,350,000. This is not good enough. There are many people who apply to the Medical Research Council. Do hon. members realize that not only medical schools apply but also veterinary colleges and they too, because they are involved in a related health science, receive grants from the council for research into animal diseases which affect both animals and humans?
The paltry $12 million in the estimates is not enough to service even the needs of our veterinary colleges. A new one has been built in Saskatchewan and has just been opened, and the amount of money needed there for research to make it a first-class centre will be tremendous.
I am happy to see the Minister of Agriculture in his seat. Perhaps he could persuade the Minister of Industry to spend a little more for improvements in veterinary schools, particularly under the aegis of the Medical Research Council. I could read editorials all night that ask the House of Commons and the government to do something about the amount of money needed for medical research.
Last March the Star-Phoenix of Saskatoon carried an editorial reading as follows:
Canada continues to drag its anchor-
I have heard other descriptions used outside this chamber.
-when it comes to support of scientific research. This is false economy and the lack of financial generosity for research is one of the root causes of the continuing "brain-drain" under which the United States gets the cream of Canada's intellectual crop.
This must have been said tens of thousands of times across the country in newspapers, over radio and television, and in this house. Yet the message has not got through and I am concerned about this.
A few weeks ago I spent some time visiting the medical college in Saskatoon. I have spoken about it previously, and I was appalled at the lack of facilities and the lack of research in depth because of the shortage of personnel and money to provide such research in depth. I have previously said that in modern times research cannot be done in a garret. You must have a research team so that if one drops out you have a back-up man to take his place. You need a whole team to do such research 23033-635
Supply-Industry
and you need proper buildings in which to do it. It is from such research that we get good teachers.
The Saskatchewan medical school, one of the newest medical schools in Canada, was brought into being when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was premier of Saskatchewan, and I am sure that if he went through it today he would be appalled at what he would see there. Let me give a few specific examples. There was a washroom for the ladies on the third floor. It is now a laboratory because they did not have space to build another laboratory, and so now the ladies must walk down two floors. Perhaps that is funny but I think it is pretty pathetic when we do not have the facilities to provide for proper laboratory space.
The school has a classroom in which 90 to 110 students are taught at a time, depending on the classes being taught. It is the only classroom on the anatomy floor. There are 70 seats and there is no room for any more. I asked Dr. Federoff, who is professor of anatomy, "What do you do with the extra students?" He replied, "We have been wondering about that too." But he is a cheerful man and he told me, "We have finally managed to snag an assistant professor of anatomy. I only hope he does not find out what it is like before he gets here." The professor added, "We ran into a problem because we did not have an office for him. There was not a nook or cranny where we could put him, so we have decided to take the end of the corridor, partition it off, and that will be his office."
Then he asked me, "Would you like to see the electron microscope we have here?" It is the only one on the campus of the university and is used by all departments. I said I would be delighted to see it and I was then taken through the dissecting room. As a physician that did not bother me very much. I spent many happy hours in such a room during my student days. But the point is that we had to walk through that room the same as technicians do and any other workers from some of the, shall we say, less bloody sciences. Then we went into a little corner room where they keep the electron microscope-this, Mr. Chairman, in this great Canada of ours where we are supposed to have all the modern things of science.
Nevertheless it is encouraging to know that despite these shabby circumstances and despite the paucity of funds this university, as is the case with many of our universities, has attained an international reputation for the

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
quality of the work done there. But this is no credit to the governments of our country. It is a credit to the few dedicated teacher-scientists who are doing this work despite the hardships under which they labour.
Some time ago I received a letter from the head of the department of physiology and pharmacology at the University of Saskatchewan, Dr. L. B. Jaques. His letter is not relevant to this discussion except in one respect. He sent me a clipping taken from the May 14 edition of the Toronto Star, with a story reported by the Canadian Press about the difficulty one doctor in Kingston had in obtaining grants from the Medical Research Council. This man, Dr. Basmajian, said that his original application for a grant was turned down because his project was termed completely impractical, and another doctor had termed it silly. The story concluded:
Dr. Basmajian said refusal of the grant obliged him to stop trying to harness nerves to artificial limbs.
The doctor was rather upset because apparently the Russians had come out with something good along this line and had announced it to the world. The only reason Dr. Jaques wrote to me was that at the time Dr. Bas-majian's application was turned down Dr. Jaques was a member of the medical advisory committee of the National Research Council, and he wanted to correct the impression Dr. Basmajian had left that his application was turned down because his project was silly.
I would like to read from this letter-I have had permission to do so-to show the real cause of refusal with respect to this remarkable project designed to help those who are disabled. Dr. Jaques says in his letter:
[DOT]-I would like to point out that Dr. Basmajian's application was refused, basically because there was not sufficient money to provide support for medical research. With money only sufficient to support one-third of the applications with well-conceived and well-planned projects-
I will repeat that:
With money only sufficient to support about one-third of the applications with well-conceived and well-planned projects, any misunderstanding or misreading of the application by the referee leading to adverse comments such as those cited by Dr. Basmajian, automatically led to the rejection of the application.
In other words, even with projects of great worth, if they find the slightest excuse they throw them away. Dr. Jaques continues:
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I have received identical treatment and it has only been by obtaining support from U.S. public

health services, has it been possible for me to continue with my research.
In a western Canadian university we find a person who has to go to the United States public health service to obtain sufficient funds not even to initiate research but to continue the research he has been doing on anti-coagulants. This is some of the most important research which is being done in this country. I might add that it was also being done by the Charles E. Frosst Company of Canada at that time through a small grant from the Medical Research Council. He continues, referring to the treatment given himself and Dr. Basmajian:
However, I do not attribute this treatment to the shortsightedness of referees but to the fact that they were forced to do an impossible job as honestly as they know how. Until the amount of money allotted annually by parliament to the Medical Research Council is approximately equal to the medical research resources of Canada, such unfortunate events will continue to happen.
I think this is most significant. This is from a member of the advisory committee to the National Research Council, and I think his comments are most apropos to the discussion this evening. I am not going to say too much more except to point out a couple of things. I have here a telegram that was sent to the Minister of Finance on September 9, 1968. It came about as a result of his statement that the government was going to put the brakes on with regard to medical research. From the comments of the minister earlier I am hopeful that the brakes are being released somewhat.
I was disturbed recently when I saw this statement by the Canadian Heart Foundation:
The provisional committee of the Canadian Association for the Advancement of the Health Sciences is alarmed at the disastrous consequences that would flow from any restraint, even temporary, on the growth of research in Canada. More particularly, we draw your attention to the need to recruit over one thousand teacher-scientists in the health fields to staff our universities in the next five years. Research is essential to the recruitment of this personnel.
We reaffirm the recommendations of the Gundy report as necessary to change the climate of medical research in Canada and urge the government to give an early indication of its long-term plans for a drive for medical manpower.
The reference to medical manpower is from the report of the royal commission on health services. We have heard nothing about that, but I hope the long-term plans in respect of research will be accelerated in a short time. The report, "Medical Research in Canada", points out at page 39 that of the grants made by the Medical Research Council grants-in-aid
November 17, 1966

have been the single most important component of the council's program since its inception and that at $7 million in 1965-66 they will be about three quarters of all expenditures. They go on to discuss what this means. I read from paragraph 3 on the same page:
In general, the pattern is that sufficient funds are available to support in full only one-third of the value of all applications; that one-half of the value of all applications can be supported only at a level of two-thirds of the funds requested; and that the balance of applications that are rejected contains projects worthy of support.
In other words, there are not sufficient funds. It seems to me that if we are going to increase the funds right now by only one-third there will still not be enough money for grants-in-aid alone. I am sure that if the government had prepared this report they would have spent more money on just getting out the report. It was handed to the government as a fait accompli, and I think that in gratitude we could supply some extra funds this year. There is one group which does have difficulty. Under the present system new grants are not made except in very exceptional circumstances. On page 44 of the report there is a comment which I think is very important:
For these grants, the shortage of funds Is even more clearly apparent: full approval could generally only be given to one-fifth of the number of applications and one-tenth of the value. About one-half of the applications have been approved in part, but the extent of this partial approval has only been about three-fifths of the amount requested.
The next paragraph on this page reads:
The inadequacy of support that can be given to new grants is particularly serious, since it is under this category of support that new entrants to medical research who have yet to make their reputation will generally be seeking funds to start their careers. The low availability of funds can only act as a severe discouragement to their efforts and as a deterrent to others contemplating entering the field of research.
I think this is a very serious statement in a report as comprehensive as the Gundy report. It is a very serious matter if we do not do something soon to try to narrow the gap between the funds available and the medical research resources which are available in Canada today. Surely the events of the past few months, and even of the past few days, would indicate the need to encourage younger people to come into the field of medical research. It is vitally important that we do this.
I know that from the graduating class at the University of Saskatchewan medical school the number of graduates who stay in Canada is so small that the situation has become 23033-635J
Supply-Industry
extremely serious indeed. In order to get interns to stay in the hospitals in the province very large inducements have to be offered. We have not been able to match those offered south of the border. We have not been able to even keep close. With all due respect to those who come to us as immigrants, and we need as many trained persons as possible, it seems a strange paradox, in a city with a medical school, that in one of the large metropolitan hospitals not one intern was educated in the province of Saskatchewan medical school. They have come from the Philippines, India, China and other countries.
I question very much whether we have the moral right to continue to attract physicians from seriously under-doctored countries. I question very much whether we have the moral right to allow our own young men and women to go south of the border-the brain drain as it is called. We are losing the very lifeblood of our country when we allow these people, because of the inducement of more benefits and greater facilities, to go there. We cannot keep them because we do not have sufficient funds. We have sufficient funds to build a $300 million edifice for defence, although the forces seem to be disintegrating. We do not have enough to keep the young people of our country here where they should be helping to educate others and look after not only our families but those of generations to come. I think it is of vital importance that we find more money and find it soon.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The very day that the Minister of Finance was talking in this house last September, the head of the Economic Council of Canada was speaking in Montreal and he said that the one thing we must not do is cut back on education or research. As he was saying this, the minister was quietly whittling away. We must increase the amounts for research and education. They go hand in hand at the university level; you cannot separate them. I think it is of vital importance that something be done immediately in this field.
In conclusion I should like to read another of the summaries of which the Gundy report is full. On page 45 of the report we find the following:
The granting experience of the Medical Research Council illustrates the problems that exist in the field of medical research in Canada. The council, within the limitations of the funds at its disposal, has apparently attempted to provide for the increasing numbers of individuals engaging in medical research at all levels of skill and experience, and to provide funds for their operations and for the

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
necessary equipment in a manner which will give some continuity of support and permit investigators to continue to work in the field.
In saying this the report gives credit to the work that has been done by the Medical Research Council, which I think has done a magnificent job in the circumstances. The key phrase in the passage I have read refers to continuity of support to permit investigators to continue to work in this field. Many of our grants are for one year, and by the time a researcher starts up and trains an assistant the grant has expired and is not continued. Something must be done to change this pattern so that investigators and researchers can obtain a bulk grant with which they can plan their projects for a two or three-year period and thereby avoid the hiring and training of new assistants all the time. The report says further:
Deficiencies exist, however, at all levels and in all categories of support and it is apparent that these deficiencies stem more from a shortage of funds than from lack of scientific merit in the applications.
I trust that the minister will take this passage to heart and will do everything in his power, as I am sure he will, to provide more funds for this most vital of all things in this country, namely, the work of the Medical Research Council and education and training in our medical schools.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity this evening to speak on the subject of Medical Research Council scholarships and grants in aid of medical research. The estimate in this respect is $12,350,000. Inasmuch as this is Thursday, November 17, four days before Monday, November 21, when the government of which I am happy to be a member will be making the largest single contribution toward medical research that the Dominion of Canada has ever known, I am glad of this opportunity to take part in the debate. On Monday afternoon the federal government, through the Minister of Veterans Affairs, will be turning over Sunnybrook hospital, with its surrounding acres and acres of grounds to the University of Toronto.
I do not know what estimate one would place on the value of that magnificent hospital and its parkland setting. No doubt the Minister of Industry could tell us how many tens of millions of dollars it is worth. However, Mr. Chairman, this hospital is being turned over to the University of Toronto for the training of doctor and for medical research. It seems rather odd that on this Thursday afternoon and evening we have had three members

of the official opposition standing up and demanding more co-operation from the federal government in the matter of medical research and student training when the education of doctors is primarily a provincial matter. I sincerely hope that the governments of Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan will learn of the well-delivered remarks of representatives of those three provinces in this house today, because their remarks could better be addressed to the provincial legislatures rather than the dominion house.
We are told that the federal government are increasing the grants in aid and scholarships in medical research from $9,250,000 last year to $12,350,000 this year. This is a fine increase, the opposition say, "but". There is always the "but" when the opposition are commenting on something that the government is doing for the good of the country. One of the speakers in this debate told us we are only stoking up the fire and are not really throwing fuel into the furnace. I would point out that in the four paragraphs of the estimates for the National Research Council, including the Medical Research Council, we have an increase of only 20 per cent in all four votes, but in the field of the Medical Research Council the increase is 33J per cent. In the four votes in these estimates the greatest increase percentagewise is in respect of the Medical Research Council, amounting to $3,100,000.
The continual demand on the federal government to enter the field of education becomes a little wearisome when you realize that several provinces are everlastingly raising their guard against the federal government intruding into the field of education. This is certainly an area in which we must make progress slowly because of the opposition from the individual provinces.
The criticisms made this afternoon by the opposition regarding the fine action that has been taken by the Pearson administration fall harshly on my ears in view of the fact that I know on Monday we are making this contribution which runs into tens of millions of dollars to the University of Toronto.
However, Mr. Chairman, what are the first words in Toronto that greet me, a member from Toronto, about Sunnybrook hospital? The first thing I hear is: Oh, it will take the doctors four years to work Sunnybrook hospital up to the requirements they set for a hospital in which they are going to teach students and in which research will be carried out. It strikes me, as a layman, as mighty funny that these people in Toronto are willing
November 17, 1966

to allow the war veterans in Sunnybrook hospital to be treated the way they are treated today-it is a magnificent hospital with magnificent facilities-and yet the moment we are turning it over for research and the training of medical students they tell us it will take four years for the doctors to bring this magnificent hospital up to the standards they have set.
In turning this hospital over to the university the Liberal administration of the day is following a recommendation of the Glassco report. The Glassco Commission was set up by our predecessors in office, the Diefenbaker government. I think it shows the breadth of wisdom of this government when I point out that we are gladly adopting the recommendation made by the Glassco commission in this regard. We not only believe that it will be a great aid to medical research in Ontario and Canada, and a great aid in training medical students, but it will be of great benefit in providing civilian beds for the city of Toronto.
The Glassco reports points out that with the success of the various provincial hospital plans, which were initiated on a national scale by the Secretary of State for External Affairs following their success in Saskatchewan under the Douglas administration and in the province of British Columbia, and in view of the success of the ten provincial hospital schemes, many beds are being left empty in veterans hospitals at the moment because men choose to stay in their local city hospitals, where they are close to relatives and friends rather than to distant veterans hospitals. The Glassco's Commission recommended that these empty beds be used for civilian purposes, since the records show that they have been empty for years on end. This Liberal administration has been happy to adopt that suggestion.
When it comes to providing funds for medical research, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that quite a few hospitals in the Dominion of Canada which have large endowments which they spend, they say, on medical research, and some hospitals that do not have large endowments, are out seeking funds for this purpose.
I for one maintain that medical research is not a function of hospitals. I can get into plenty of arguments on that score with doctors on the staffs of hospitals that have endowments.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Of course these gentlemen maintain that there is nobody as brilliant as they are and
Supply-Industry
that they alone should have the right to say how the endowments that they enjoy shall be spent in research. I believe that research should be under the auspices of universities. It is interesting to know that one of the Commonwealth countries in the southern hemisphere introduced about two years ago legislation impressing endowments made to hospitals for medical research to be used under the auspices of universities. This is the subject of lively discussions in the southern hemisphere at the present time and it is becoming a very lively topic of discussion in hospital and university circles in Canada. There is no reason under the sun why certain hospitals, which over a period of 80, 90 or 100 years have built up a tremendous reputation in this field and are now enjoying continuous gifts, particularly through sums bequeathed to them, should be able to spend funds for research carried out by their closed staffs as distinct from medical research grants to universities. If those endowment funds were taken over by individual provinces and applied to medical research in university centres the money could be used for the good of many universities and many research specialists instead of being used for a few hospitals, few researchers and few doctors.
The hon. member for Saskatoon referred to the shortage of interns. I know of one particular hospital where the interns employed by this hospital are assigned to certain doctors in that hospital which is richly endowed. These doctors tell the interns to do research for them so as to build up the doctor's reputation, taking advantage of the money which was bequeathed by people long since dead and gone. I do not believe that doctors on the staff of public hospitals should be allowed to build up a reputation for themselves by using what I consider to be public funds which were left in wills and on which no succession duties were turned over to the government. I do not believe the day is far distant when the endowments left to hospitals will be taken over by the provinces and used for medical research carried out by universities for the good of the whole country.
In commending the government for its action in increasing the grants to the Medical Research Council by 33J per cent, which is an invasion into provincial jurisdiction, I should like to express my thanks for the decision taken by this party and this government to turn Sunnybrook Hospital over to the University of Toronto for the training of medical students and for research. I should

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
also like to commend the government for the size of the contribution made to medical research in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened very closely to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) when he dealt with the importance of the National Research Council, including the Medical Research Council. The hon. member mentioned several times that the federal government was not allocating sufficient money so that such research may be more consistent with the needs of the country.
The hon. member for Saskatoon, himself a doctor, was entirely right when he said that we are short of money, that we should find the required money; that we spend too much for national defence, when we should be spending more in the medical or national field.

The statement of the hon. member for Saskatoon is therefore inconsistent with the activities of his own party in the last three weeks. Well, Mr. Chairman, 1 fully agree with the hon. member-

The hon. member said,
"a monument". This is an affirmation, not a question. I should like the hon. member to ask me a question if he has one to ask.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand the hon. member for Saskatoon to mean that a

building now under construction or about to be built will probably cost the government millions of dollars. However, that building will nevertheless be used by the Canadian armed forces.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
And the hon. member for Saskatoon will agree with me that for the last three weeks, his political party has been against reducing the expenditures of the National Defence Department through unification of the Canadian armed forces. And the hon. member is aware that those expenditures will be sharply reduced when we have one army instead of three.
Now, when the hon. member talks about the construction of an army building anywhere in Canada, he has the right to do so.
I do it myself, and I even feel that we spend too much now for national defence. And, like the hon. member also, I feel that we spend far from enough in the field of research.
And when you consider that vote 10 of the National Research Council, including the Medical Research Council, amounts to $41 million, I think that any member of the house feels that $41 million, even if it is a huge amount, is not enough to help research in this country.
When you consider, Mr. Chairman, that this year we will pay in interest only on the public debt $1,215 million without touching the principal. That is 29.5 times the amount allocated to the National Research Council including the Medical Research Council.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) did not mention that. And I do not think that the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) will mention it now or when we reach the end of the estimates of the department now under consideration.
But, Mr. Chairman, the same problems exist throughout the world. Yesterday, it is not so long ago, on November 16, Mr. Daniel Johnson, premier of Quebec, received at his office a group of senior Swedish officials-this means that those people came for Sweden-and I want that to be recorded in Hansard, so that everyone will understand, even the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay). As I said, some Swedish officials came to pay him a courtesy call. After that, at a conference, Mr. Gunnar Lange-I do not know how it is pronounced in Swedish but it is Lange, and I thank the former minister of immigration for telling me that the name is
November 17, 1966

Lange-the minister of trade from Sweden, said that Mr. Johnson had asked them if they could not give him a steel plant. At the present time, Sweden has 64 steel plants and it is a country smaller than the province of Quebec. The 64 steel plants operated by the private sector are showing a profit whereas the 65th, operated by the state, shows a deficit.
Mr. Gunnar Lange said that if it were up to him to decide, he would give up the Swedish state iron foundry to the province of Quebec, but not the ironworks under private enterprise, for the latter have a profit earning capacity while the state enterprise shows a deficit.
And to think that we have here people who are ready to spend millions of dollars for research, as if the federal government or provincial ones were willing to assume the responsibility of developing existing industries and creating new ones. We made an attempt in Quebec with Sidbec, but it was not very successful.
I see my colleague from Matapedia-Ma-tane (Mr. Tremblay); he knows full well that Sidbec was not really a success.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that if governments, present or future federal governments, or provincial governments, were to pay more attention to private industry in order to stimulate personal initiative, solutions would be found to the problems which crop up from day to day.
As for item 10, the funds for the National Research Council, including those for the Medical Research Council, it amounts to $41,000,000, that is 29 times less than the interest we pay on the national debt. Yet, the National Research Council is far more important than the interest we can and must pay on the national debt. But no one seems to worry much about it, and the debate goes on.
A while ago, the member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) repeated many times again: How is it that we have no money, no credits, no finance? It is always the same problem. No money, no finance; we are broke and there is very little that we see through to the end. We vote supply this year, and we will do the same next year, going on and on in the same fashion, without change, without initiative, tossed about as we are by a financial system which is clearly old fashioned in this day and age.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have had a good debate about the National Research Council and specialized research. I will approach the minister on a broader basis. We have heard and we know that the National Research Council makes grants, as the hon. member for York-Humber said, toward medical research. We support scientific research, but many research projects from time to time are duplicated. By and large the National Research Council disburses money, trying to put every dollar to good use. What we have failed to introduce in this country and what we desperately need is more applied research. Nobody downgrades the importance of specialized or pure scientific research, but applied research is something we have not debated and my recommendations are directed to that field.
In broad terms, applied research can effect every department of government. Let us consider the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which gathers a great deal of information. Unless that information is put to practical use it is of little value. The government of this country spends more money buying goods than any other corporation or individual within the country. Yet we rely to a great extent on pure extinct in deciding what to buy and where to spend money. Consider the organization known as the Japanese Export Trade Research Organization, JETRO for short. It is no accident that the Japanese have cornered about 67 per cent of the Canadian and United States stainless steelware market, nor is it an accident that most members of the press gallery have good cameras made in Japan. This situation has been brought about through a careful research program.
The JETRO people subcontract their market research to individuals or companies in Canada, the United States, Germany and so on. When that research is finished they know what Canadians like, whether the articles are cameras or pieces of luggage. They know the weight, the colour and the style of luggage that will sell here. They know who the buyers are, whether they are good or bad bargainers,
November 17, 1966

whether they belong to clubs and, if so, what clubs. As a result when a Japanese salesman comes to Canada to sell luggage he knows exactly what to sell and how to sell it and the manufacturers in Japan know what to produce. This sort of thing happened with stainless steelware. The Japanese have concentrated on applied research whereas we have not. We try to sell the wrong goods to countries at the wrong prices because we do not have the facts.
Comprehensive research under the National Research Council can be developed, and I shall make suggestions about that. We have heard much about the export of gas but we do not really know how long gas will be a source of energy before being replaced by atomic or other forms of energy. We have preserved our coal resources and we are stuck with a great deal of coal in the ground that we cannot use. We built the St. Lawrence canal system but we did not find out the future requirements of water transport, the size that ships will be or whether they will be able to unload in our ports. So we are now duplicating canals and locks, and we are not making money. The ships are getting larger and larger and we do not know if we will be able to accommodate them.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We have heard a great deal about specific problems, including housing, sewage disposal and in fact every field of endeavour, but we judge by instinct even though there is a very sophisticated method of getting the facts and applying them in future programs. In the United States the Rand Corporation does the research work and advises the United States armed forces, industry and the finance department in Washington. It is a very good organization, and by using such a tool of sophisticated research not just in a narrow field we could do a good deal for all government departments.
What I envisage is a crown corporation employing the best brains we have in Canada, a well-staffed organization to be at the beck and call of each and every department of the federal government, and the provincial governments and municipalities. It should be provided with all the necessary facilities and the best equipment. The organization would produce results whereby, if the Minister of Industry, for instance, wanted to know whether to stockpile more atomic fuel for future use in electric energy, it could tell him that in all probability within ten years, using the facilities they had, they could develop an electric
Supply-Industry
power plant suitable for any size of requirement in any community of any nation. The minister would then know what policy to adopt with respect to raw materials and with respect to aid for industry.
I think all hon. members will agree that we are living in a very sophisticated age so far as research is concerned. It is no longer sensible merely to guess. We should have the proper facilities and, as I say, a crown corporation to be at the call of governments at all levels, and of private industry, so that each specific problem can be researched and an answer given in broad terms in order that the results of that research can be applied to our problems as we face them from time to time.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is significant to me that on the other side of the house there are as many doctors who are members of parliament as there are on this side and yet none of them have been able to defend or even attempt to defend this pittance that is being used as an excuse for producing medical research in Canada. The hon. member for Villeneuve has said that the party to which I belong is a socialist one. I say in reply that there is no other expenditure the government makes that represents more the welfare of all the people of Canada than does the amount that is spent on medical research.
Medical research is not a matter of buildings donated to the cause of medical research, nor is it a matter of salary for the people who are producing this research. Rather it is the funds that are necessary to carry on the research in the buildings that already exist and to provide such facilities whereby we are going to retain our research people within this country rather than lose them to the country south of us as we have been doing for so many years.
Recently in the press we have read that the Minister of Finance is going to reduce the rate of increase of the amount to be spent on medical research. It is my understanding that the amount of $15,350,000 in the present year's estimates will not be raised to the minimum amount of $23 million that has been suggested. We of the medical profession are aware that anything less than $23 million would have a devastating impact on Canada's continued progress in the field of health sciences.
It is almost incredible to think that from the list of estimated government expenditures for the year 1967-68 which could well bear drastic pruning such a fundamentally important one as this should have been selected to

November 17, 1966
Supply-Industry
be decreased. The exodus of Canadian medical teacher-scientists will be even further stimulated by the proposed cutback, and it will be impossible to attract teacher-scientists from the United States in sufficient numbers to meet the growing Canadian faculty needs. This is not too hard to understand when one considers that the present per capita expenditure for medical research in the United States amounts to $6.50 compared with a mere 90 cents in Canada. Over seven times the amount per capita that we spend is spent on medical research in the United States, and surely we are as great on a per capita basis as the United States.
The staffs of new universities at present are secured by taking teachers from existing universities. In other words, what we are doing is playing musical chairs with our highly trained personnel across Canada. What is needed is sufficient funds to keep our own trained men in this country.
Of the scientists who take up permanent residence in the United States 10 per cent are Canadians but 23 per cent give Canada as their last address. So we are rapidly becoming a good way-station en route to a country which has adequate funds for medical research. Naturally, Mr. Chairman, this is going to attract the best brains to the country to the south of us, not because of salary but because they know they will have enough money to carry on their work and not have to stop in the middle of it. These figures prove there is a full-scale crisis right at this moment in Canada.
What needs to be said about this has been much more adequately said by many experts in this field, people who are wiser in this respect than I am, and in that context I would like to quote first from a Globe and Mail editorial which appeared on September 24, 1966:
Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp's plea for greater restraint in the rate of research grant increases as an anti-inflationary measure might lead one to believe that in the field of medicine, for example, research could fairly be regarded as a peripheral activity in the work of providing medical care and training doctors; that it is a dispensable adjunct to the main operation and can be painlessly amputated.
The nation must learn to pace itself, we are told. Quite so, but how should this be applied in the area of medical research?
Four men who are, in their individual ways, concerned in medical research and training, give views in The Globe magazine today which suggest that restraining medical research funds could be one of the most ill-conceived economies in the history of Canadian medicine, and that it could condemn Canada to at least a decade of second-class medical care.

There is a striking similarity in the opinions offered by the four: Dr. Louis Siminovitch, head of the division of biological research, Ontario Cancer Institute; Dr. John Armstrong, executive director of the Canadian Heart Foundation; Dr. John Evans, dean of medicine at McMaster University; and Mr. Edward Dunlop, member of the legislature for Forest Hill and executive director of the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society.
Each in turn acknowledges the fact that if Canada does not move boldly ahead with the provision of much larger research funds than are now being dispensed, the impact will be felt heavily-and for a number of years-upon the calibre of medical teachers that can be recruited and consequently upon the standards of our future doctors.
The urgency of the matter stems, ironically, from the federal government's provision of a $500 million health resources fund, set up to provide physical facilities for medical training. Thus, four new medical schools will come into operation within a few years and expansions will take place at established schools.
The task of recruiting department heads and staff for the new schools is an immediate one and there are compelling reasons for filling the positions with men of the highest quality. This, the experts are agreed, is an impossible task with the resources they have to hand.
Dr. Evans explains: "People just will not take full time positions in university departments unless they can continue their research-
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
At present we need people with the research approach, not so much for the discoveries that they are going to make, but because they are updating their knowledge and are in a position to act as continuing educators ... It is almost impossible for them to maintain their interest, their contacts, their flow of information, the updating of their knowledge without doing research.
I have quoted only part of this editorial, but I wish to emphasize the quotation from Dr. Evans of McMaster University in Hamilton. This of course is of great interest to myself. Dr. Evans is one of the most promising and progressive doctors of any medical faculty in Canada. Although this university is only in the making in so far as a medical college is concerned, they fully expect to be able to open a medical school in 1969. Already there are pre-medical students elsewhere in McMaster University. The success of the medical college is dependent on the amount of the grant from the government to enable them to acquire teachers for this great university.
As I have said before, we have the buildings and we have the necessary physical attributes to carry on a medical school but we do not have the teaching personnel nor the incentive to attract them. How are we going to get these teachers? Are we going to take them from other universities and deplete their staff? Are we going to do without? Or we
November 17, 1966

going to get second-rate teachers because all our professors and men of learning have gone to the United States and are not here in this country to teach simply for the reason that there was not enough money for medical research in this country?
One of the bodies which is greatly interested in medical research is the Association of Medical Colleges of Canada, a relatively newly formed body. They met in Saskatoon last September. They had a convention with representatives from all parts of Canada and from all medical colleges of Canada. Also within this body are the College of General Practice of Canada, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Association of Hospital Administrators, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation and the Canadian Association for Advancement of Health Sciences.
A letter was sent to the Prime Minister of this country by Mr. Gundy who is known for the Gundy report on medical research. It contains another 14 pages of names of prominent people such as deans and assistant deans from universities all across Canada. At the meeting in Saskatoon these people drew up a resolution which I do not believe has been released. I should like to read it into the record because of the significance of the people who constitute this body and because of the conclusions this massive body came to in this regard. The title is "Support Of Medical Research". It reads:
In Canada the shortage of physicians of all kinds, especially those that provide family care, is alarming. The 12 existing medical schools and the 4 new ones are committed to the formidable task of increasing the number of places for undergraduates, graduates, and physicians in continuing education programs. At the same time they must upgrade the quality of their training programs. This objective- producing the many kinds of health workers needed in the future-can only be reached if the numbers of teachers and medical scientists now employed In Canadian medical schools more than doubles over the next five years. If Canadian medical schools are to retain good teachers and scientists, attract others from abroad, and induce larger numbers of talented students to continue in academic careers, adequate facilities and greatly increased funds to cover the operating costs for research must be provided.
The Association of Canadian Medical Colleges and other medical groups in Canada have for some years urged greater federal government support for research in medical schools. In 1965 the report entitled "Medical Research in Canada" (Gundy Report) presented a comprehensive estimate of capital and operating funds needed to support research at a reasonable level in Canadian medical schools during the period 1966-1970. As far as can be predicted the health resources fund should meet
Supply-Industry
the need for capital expenditures although the delay in passing specific legislation has held up the construction of badly needed facilities. Similarly, the new programs of the Medical Research Council, made possible by the special 65 per cent increase in its budget for 1966-67, seemed to indicate that the federal government recognized the urgent need for support of medical research. However, much of the benefit of the Medical Research Council budget increase may be lost if the announcement of the Minister of Finance on September 8, 1966 to "exercise more restraint" on the rate of increase of research support is implemented. We are nevertheless concerned to re-emphasize the dependence of quality of health care on medical research and the necessity to create, without delay, a favourable climate and a stable environment for medical research in Canada.
Over the next five years Canadian medical schools have goals that will require over 1,200 new teachers and medical scientists. Unless staff of high quality are obtained we will lose a unique opportunity to upgrade markedly the standard of medical education and health care in Canada. The most important consideration in attracting staff of requisite quality today is the adequacy of support for medical research.
This is the nub of the whole thing.
In the light of these considerations the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges reaffirms its conviction that strong scientific programs in medical schools and their teaching hospitals are essential to high standards of undergraduate, graduate and continuing medical education and-in the final analysis-to quality health care. In the present phase of rapid expansion of facilities for medical education the need for a consistent policy of greatly increased support for medical research is essential. Failure to develop such a policy of greatly increased support for medical research makes it increasingly difficult for the medical schools to attract teachers and scientists. This places in jeopardy the future standard of health care for Canadians. Resolution
Whereas the shortage of all kinds of physicians, especially those that provide family care, is alarming;
Whereas there are not enough high quality medical teachers and scientists to staff existing medical schools and to man new and expanded facilities;
Whereas there is an urgent need for funds for research and development to attract and keep such teachers and scientists;
Whereas teachers and scientists of the greatest competence must be obtained without delay in order to train adeuate numbers of physicians;
Whereas in comparison to sums spent in other government programs, expenditures in support of medical research are small; however, these expenditures will exert a profound influence on medical education and future health care;
And whereas the Minister of Finance has recently announced a reduction in the projected rate of increase in funds for research;
Be it resolved that the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges emphatically recommend that funds for medical research be substantially increased until the objectives recommended by the Gundy report are reached. These can be achieved

November 17, 1966
Royal Assent
by adoption of the revised Medical Research Council budget for 1966-67 as a base, and acceptance of the recommendation of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, based on the formula of the Bladen Report, of (a) an additional 30 per cent for administration, (b) a grant of 10 per cent of salaries to each institution as a general encouragement for research and (c) an annual rate of growth in research grants of 50 per cent, as communicated to the Prime Minister, May 30, 1966.
Only such significant increases in support of medical research will assure the required change in the climate of research in Canada so that defects in the quantity and quality of medical manpower can be repaired.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-SEARCH OF PRIVATE HOMES
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-SEARCH OF PRIVATE HOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to raise a matter today, about which I put a question two days ago and received no answer. My question was directed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) responsible for the R.C.M.P. I do not see him in the house tonight and I wonder who will answer. I even wonder whether there is somebody to answer. Ah. I see there is a substitute who will answer the question.

DEBATES	November 17, 1968
Here is the case, Mr. Speaker. Last Thursday, that is on November 10, about 8 o'clock p.m., when Mr. Jean-Louis Denoncourt, 264 St. Charles St. West, Longueuil, had just left his residence, three police constables, one from the R.C.M.P., one from the Quebec provincial police and another from the Montreal municipal police, having search warrant No. 21947, entered into Mr. Denoncourt's house. These policemen were posted around his house, waiting for him to leave, in order to get in with the search warrant I just mentioned. On entering, they read it out rapidly to Denoncourt's young sister, a 17-year old, who could not quite make out what they were reading so fast. The policemen even refused to show her the document. According to Denoncourt's sister, the policemen were very rude to her as well as to her friend, Raymond Larouche who was at Denoncourt's home at this time.
I should like to mention at this point that Jean-Louis Denoncourt is the regional director of the Rassemblement pour l'independance nationale, which political party is legally recognized as such in the province of Quebec. It is not that this party advocates the independence of Quebec, for it is not the same party as the Ralliement national. In fact, they are competitors after a fashion. But that is not why I am bringing up the matter. I do so because I feel that the treatment inflicted upon a partisan of independence, where members of the R.C.M.P. were involved, should not recur. I believe in democracy and feel that the police should not interfere with political matters.
And so, the policemen asked to go into the house and more specifically to go into Jean-Louis Denoncourt's bedroom. They went in, pulled out the drawers and emptied them on the floor in a heap that begs description. In the meantime, they refused access to the apartment to everyone, and prevented-which they did not have the right to do-Denoncourt's sister from putting in a telephone call to one of her uncles, Dollard Dansereau, a very well known Montreal lawyer.
When Miss Denoncourt tried to make a phone call, one of the policemen put his hand on the phone so as to prevent her from using it, which is something completely irregular. This was repeated many times.
The policemen were especially looking for papers, files belonging to the executives of the organization for the Richelieu area of the Rassemblement pour l'independance nationale.
November 17, 1966
At one moment, Miss Denoncourt succeeded in shutting herself up in a room, with the telephone, and in getting in touch with another brother of Mr. Denoncourt, who is a teacher and lives in Longueuil.
When he reached the home of Mr. Jean-Louis Denoncourt, the police officers almost denied him entry, requiring him beforehand to identify himself before entering his brother's home, which is quite an abnormal situation.
When Mr. Denoncourt's mother arrived, the police officers were openly rude to her, yet she had nothing to do with the whole matter.
They seized indiscriminately all the political literature of the R.I.N. found at Mr. Denoncourt's, including a great deal of official information regarding the election campaign conducted by Mr. Denoncourt in the Laviolette riding, as well as the names of all those who worked in that election.
Following such action, Mr. Speaker, I would like to know who laid that complaint against Mr. Denoncourt. What kind of complaint was it? The police officers said they were looking for explosives but they did not find any. They left with the records of the political organization called the Rassemblement pour l'in-dependance nationale.
I would like to know what the police officers were looking for. I would like to know if they found what they were looking for. I would like to know if the police officers took something else besides what they were looking for, and I would like to know also what they took with them. Did they give everything back to the owner? Did they find anything improper in Mr. Denoncourt's home? Has such a search been made at the same Mr. Denoncourt's home over the last two years? If so, who had laid the complaint? Did they find anything improper during those previous searches? On what were the complaints based at the time of the previous searches? I would also like to know the names of the police officers who made the search on November 10, 1966. Which police force obtained the search warrant? Why was the Royal Canadian Mounted Police there? Who had asked for or authorized them to be there? Were the seized documents photographed, and who has the pictures of the documents?
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I ask these questions, Mr. Speaker, because there was a flagrant violation of a man's property simply because he is involved with political organization. I feel that a man may be a partisan of independence without having
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion political and electoral organization documents seized in his home.
I wish to protest against what has happened. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police were there, they did not object to preventing a young lady from calling a lawyer and another person from coming to his brother's home, and to acting impolitely toward that young lady's mother. Why did the Royal Canadian Mounted Police let that happen?
And do not tell me that such information is not ordinarily available, because public inquiries have been made in several such cases. But, because a partisan of independence is involved, people try to hide everything.
Let there be no hypocrisy, do not refuse to answer, let straight answers be given to the questions I have just asked.
